title: Depreciation and Amortisation
outcomes: Explain what depreciation is (and is not), why it is charged and what causes it.
Work out the cost of an item of property, plant and equipment (PPE), its depreciable amount and useful life, including component accounting.
Compute depreciation under the straight line, written down value, sum of years' digits, machine hour, production units and depletion methods, with part-year periods.
Record depreciation with and without a provision for depreciation account, and compute profit or loss on disposal using an asset disposal account.
Account for a change in method, useful life or residual value (as a change in estimate) and for revaluation of PPE.
Define intangible assets, apply the recognition conditions and compute amortisation.

meta.exam_tip: A 10-mark machinery account with additions and a sale is a favourite. Keep an asset-wise working note, charge part-year depreciation by months, and depreciate the sold asset up to the date of sale before working out the profit or loss.

concepts.title: What depreciation is
body: Property, plant and equipment (PPE) are tangible items held for use in producing or supplying goods or services, for renting to others or for administration, and expected to be used for more than twelve months — machinery, buildings, vehicles, furniture. They are recorded at cost and help earn revenue (or save cost) over many years.

Depreciation spreads the depreciable amount of such an asset — its cost (or revalued amount) less its residual value — over its useful life in a systematic way. Schedule II to the Companies Act, 2013 describes it in these terms. Useful life is the period over which the entity expects to use the asset, or the number of units it expects to produce with it.
Causes of fall in value: wear and tear from use; passage of time even when idle; obsolescence (technology or demand changes); fall in market value; and depletion of natural resources such as mines.

Depreciation begins when the asset is available for use — in place and in the condition management intends — even if it is not yet actually used. Each year the expired part of the cost is charged as depreciation (matching), and the unexpired part stays in the balance sheet as the carrying amount (written down value). Depreciation is an allocation of cost, not a measure of current market value.
concepts.analogy: You buy a ₹60,000 phone you expect to use for 3 years. Its "cost per year" is about ₹20,000 — that yearly share is depreciation, whatever the resale price happens to be.
concepts.work: Every company maintains a fixed asset register — asset-wise cost, date put to use, life, method, accumulated depreciation. Without it, depreciation and profit or loss on disposal cannot be computed reliably, and it is one of the first registers an auditor asks for.

concepts.title: Why depreciation is charged
body: Correct profit: the use of the asset is a real cost of earning the year's revenue; ignoring it overstates profit.
True financial position: the asset should appear at its unexpired cost, not at its original cost.

Retention of funds for replacement: depreciation reduces divisible profit, so the money is kept in the business rather than distributed — though replacement may cost more due to inflation or technology.
Correct cost of production: depreciation of factory assets is part of product cost.

Depreciation is a non-cash expense — no money leaves the business when it is charged. It does not itself create funds; it only stops profits being over-distributed. It must be charged even in a loss year.
concepts.analogy: Setting aside part of your salary each month for the next phone does not create money — it just stops you spending all of it now.
concepts.work: Lenders and analysts add depreciation back to profit to estimate cash generation (EBITDA). Understanding that depreciation is non-cash is basic to cash-flow work.

concepts.title: Measuring depreciation: cost, useful life, residual value
body: Three estimates drive the charge: cost, useful life (in years or units, based on experience, expected usage, shifts, repairs policy, technology) and residual value (what the asset is expected to fetch at the end of its life after disposal costs; treated as nil if insignificant). Depreciable amount = cost (or revalued amount) − residual value.

Cost of PPE = the price paid to the supplier, plus import duties and purchase taxes that cannot be recovered, minus trade discounts and rebates; plus costs directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition needed for its intended use; plus the initial estimate of dismantling, removal and site-restoration costs.

Directly attributable costs include employee costs arising directly from acquiring or building the asset, site preparation, initial delivery and handling, installation and assembly, testing (less the net sale proceeds of samples produced while testing), and professional fees such as engineers' charges.

Not part of cost: opening a new facility (inauguration), introducing a new product (advertising), doing business in a new place or with a new class of customers (including staff training), administration and general overheads, costs incurred while the asset is ready but idle or running below capacity, and relocation costs. Later expenditure is capitalised only if it increases life or capacity; additions are depreciated over the remaining life, and an addition with a separate identity is accounted for as a separate asset.

blocks.title: What is capitalised

concepts.analogy: Cost is everything you spent to get the machine standing in the factory and working — not the party to celebrate it, nor the advertisements for what it will make.
concepts.work: Capitalisation reviews are routine in audits: capitalising revenue items (like training or inauguration) inflates profit and assets, so each addition is vouched to invoices and the "date ready for use" is checked.

concepts.title: Component accounting
body: Both the accounting standards and Schedule II require each significant part of an asset to be depreciated separately when its cost is significant relative to the whole and its useful life or method differs from the rest.

An aircraft is the classic case: the airframe, the engines and the interiors have different lives. Parts with the same life and method may be grouped. Small parts replaced frequently can be expensed when replaced.
concepts.analogy: A car's body may last 15 years but its tyres only 3 — you would not spread the tyres' cost over 15 years.
concepts.work: When a large plant is commissioned, engineers and accountants together split the cost into components (civil works, main machinery, electricals, moulds) with separate lives in the fixed asset register.

concepts.title: Straight line and written down value methods
body: Straight line method (SLM, fixed instalment): the same amount every year. Depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life; rate = annual depreciation ÷ cost × 100. Simple and suited to assets that give equal benefit every year (leases, many plants). Weakness: repairs rise as the asset ages, so total charge (depreciation + repairs) rises over time.

Written down value method (WDV, reducing / diminishing balance): a fixed percentage of the opening carrying amount each year, so the charge falls every year. Rate = [1 − (residual value ÷ cost)^(1/n)] × 100. Heavy charge early when repairs are low, light charge later when repairs are high — roughly even total burden. The asset never reaches zero. Risks: too low a rate may leave the asset under-depreciated; residues of scrapped assets can linger if no plant register is kept. Income-tax rules use WDV (block of assets) except for certain power undertakings.
Under both methods, depreciation in the year of purchase or sale is only for the months the asset was available for use.

Recording: either credit the asset account each year (Depreciation A/c Dr, To Asset A/c), or keep the asset at cost and credit a Provision for Depreciation (accumulated depreciation) account (Depreciation A/c Dr, To Provision for Depreciation A/c). The second shows both the original investment and its carrying amount, and is preferred. In both cases Depreciation A/c is closed to the profit and loss account.

blocks.title: SLM vs WDV for the same machine

concepts.analogy: SLM is paying the same EMI every month; WDV is like a battery that loses a fixed percentage of whatever charge is left.
concepts.work: Companies often use SLM in their books (lives per Schedule II) but WDV for income tax, which creates deferred tax — a topic you will meet later. Explaining why "book depreciation" and "tax depreciation" differ is a common client conversation.

concepts.title: Other methods: SYD, machine hour, production units, depletion
body: Sum of years' digits (SYD): a variant of the reducing charge. Depreciation = depreciable amount × (remaining life at the start of the year, including that year) ÷ (sum of the digits 1 to n). For n years the sum is n(n + 1)/2. Not widely used.

Machine hour method: rate per hour = depreciable amount ÷ total estimated working hours; annual charge = hours worked × rate. It is the straight line idea applied per hour. Schedule II reflects it partly through extra depreciation for double or triple shift working of certain plant.
Production units method: depreciable amount × units produced this year ÷ total estimated units. Suitable for machines producing a uniform product.
Depletion method: for wasting assets such as mines, quarries, oil wells. Rate per unit = cost ÷ estimated total quantity extractable; charge = quantity extracted × rate.
concepts.analogy: Machine hour and production units charge "per use", like paying for a taxi by the kilometre rather than a fixed monthly rent.
concepts.work: Mining and oil companies report depletion as a major expense; reserve estimates from geologists directly change the profit for the year.

concepts.title: Disposal of an asset — profit or loss
body: When an asset is sold, first charge depreciation for the part of the year up to the date of sale. Then profit or loss = sale proceeds − carrying amount on that date. This goes to the profit and loss account.

All entries can be made in the asset account itself, or an Asset Disposal Account can be opened: transfer the asset's cost to it, transfer the accumulated depreciation (if a provision account is kept), credit the sale proceeds, and the balance is the profit or loss.
Keep an asset-wise working note — in an exam with several machines, it is the only safe way to get the right figures.
concepts.analogy: Selling your two-year-old phone: compare the price you get with the "unused" part of its cost, not with what you paid originally.
concepts.work: In software, an asset sale voucher must remove both the gross cost and the accumulated depreciation; forgetting the second leaves ghost balances in the fixed asset schedule.

concepts.title: Changes in method, useful life and residual value
body: Method, useful life and residual value are estimates and must be reviewed at least at each financial year-end.

A change in the depreciation method (made because the pattern in which the asset's benefits are consumed has changed significantly) is treated as a change in accounting estimate: the carrying amount on the date of change is depreciated under the new method from then on. Its effect is quantified and disclosed.

A change in useful life or residual value is also a change in estimate: the remaining depreciable amount (carrying amount − revised residual value) is spread over the revised remaining life. Past depreciation is not recalculated — the change is prospective.
concepts.analogy: If halfway through a road trip you learn the destination is closer, you change your speed from here on — you don't re-drive the part already covered.
concepts.work: IT companies regularly shorten laptop and server lives because of faster obsolescence; the accountant computes the higher future charge and the note on change in estimate.

concepts.title: Revaluation of PPE
body: After initial recognition, an entity may choose (it is an accounting policy, not compulsory) to carry PPE at a revalued amount — fair value at the revaluation date less later accumulated depreciation and impairment — if fair value can be measured reliably.

Rules: revalue regularly enough that carrying amounts stay close to fair value; revalue the entire class of assets, not selected items; an increase is credited to Revaluation Surplus in owners' equity — except that it goes to profit and loss to the extent it reverses an earlier decrease of the same asset charged to profit and loss; a decrease is charged to profit and loss — except that it is debited to Revaluation Surplus to the extent of any surplus already existing for that asset.

The surplus can be moved straight to retained earnings once the asset is derecognised (retired or sold), or gradually as the extra depreciation on the revalued amount is charged — never through the profit and loss account. After revaluation, depreciation is based on the revalued amount over the remaining life.
concepts.analogy: Re-pricing every flat in a building, not just the one with the best view — otherwise the picture is selective.
concepts.work: Real-estate-heavy companies that revalue land and buildings get valuers' reports; auditors check that the whole class was revalued and that the surplus did not pass through profit.

concepts.title: Intangible assets
body: An intangible asset is a non-monetary asset that can be identified separately and has no physical form, held for use in producing or supplying goods or services, for rental to others or for administration. Examples: patents, trademarks, copyrights, computer software, streaming and broadcasting rights, airport landing slots, film distribution rights, long-term customer contracts, customer databases and purchased goodwill.

It is recognised only if: it is identifiable (it could be sold, rented, licensed or exchanged separately); the entity controls it (can obtain its benefits and restrict others); future economic benefits are probable; and its cost can be measured reliably.

Cost of a separately acquired intangible = purchase price + non-recoverable duties and taxes + directly attributable costs of preparing it for use (for example legal fees), less trade discounts and rebates. It is removed from the balance sheet on disposal or when no further benefits are expected; the gain or loss (net proceeds − carrying amount) goes to profit and loss.

Tangible vs intangible: tangible assets have physical form and a life based on expected usage, and are depreciated; intangibles lack physical form, often have lives set by contract or law (purchased goodwill may even have an indefinite life), are presumed not to exceed ten years unless there is evidence otherwise, and are amortised.
concepts.analogy: A trademark is like a famous restaurant's name on the door — you can't touch its value, but you can sell or license it, and it brings customers in.
concepts.work: Valuing customer contracts, brands and software on acquisitions is a big advisory area; at Foundation level, focus on the recognition tests and amortisation.

concepts.title: Amortisation
body: Amortisation is depreciation of an intangible asset: its depreciable amount (cost − residual value) is spread systematically over the best estimate of its useful life, starting when the asset is available for use.

Useful life is presumed not to exceed ten years from the date of availability unless there is evidence to the contrary — software and similar assets may have much shorter lives; contractual rights for longer periods can be amortised over that longer period where evidence supports it.

Method should follow the pattern in which benefits are consumed; if that pattern cannot be determined reliably, use the straight line method. Residual value is assumed to be zero unless a third party has committed to buy the asset at the end of its life, or an active market exists that will give a residual value and is likely to exist at that time.
The period and method are reviewed at least at each year-end; significant changes are reflected prospectively.

concepts.analogy: A 5-year movie streaming licence is used up a little every year — amortisation records that using-up.
concepts.work: Software licences and ERP implementation costs are common intangibles in client books; auditors check the start date (available for use) and the life chosen.

illustrations.title: Change in useful life, change in method, revaluation
illustrations.q: (a) A machine costing ₹12,00,000 was depreciated on SLM over 10 years (nil residual value) for 4 years. Its remaining life is now estimated at 4 years. Depreciation for year 5? (b) An asset costing ₹10,00,000 (residual value ₹1,00,000, life 9 years) was depreciated on SLM for 3 years; from year 4 the entity switches to WDV at 20%. Depreciation for year 4? (c) Another asset with a carrying amount of ₹7,00,000 is revalued at ₹8,40,000 at the end of a year; remaining life 7 years. Treatment and next year's depreciation?

solution.title: (a) Change in useful life
solution.text: Carrying amount after 4 years = 12,00,000 − 4 × 1,20,000 = ₹7,20,000. Spread over the revised remaining life of 4 years: ₹1,80,000 a year. Past depreciation is not changed.

solution.title: (b) Change in method
solution.text: SLM charge was ₹1,00,000 a year; carrying amount after 3 years = ₹7,00,000. Year 4 under WDV = 20% × 7,00,000 = ₹1,40,000. It is a change in estimate, applied from year 4 onwards.

solution.title: (c) Revaluation
solution.text: Increase ₹1,40,000 is credited to Revaluation Surplus (equity), not to profit and loss. Next year's depreciation = 8,40,000 ÷ 7 = ₹1,20,000.

jobs.title: Reviewing capital additions in an audit
jobs.role: Articled assistant on the audit of a manufacturer
jobs.situation: The client capitalised ₹42 lakh for a new bottling line, including the inauguration function, operator training and three months of electricity while the line stood ready but waiting for orders.
steps: Vouch the supplier invoice, freight, installation and commissioning bills — these belong in cost.
Remove the inauguration, training and idle-period electricity — these are expenses of the year.
Check the "available for use" date from commissioning reports; depreciation starts from that date even if production started later.
Check whether major parts (moulds, filling heads) need separate component lives.
Agree the corrected figure to the fixed asset register and recompute depreciation.
jobs.takeaway: What goes into cost decides depreciation for years to come — errors in capitalisation repeat every year until the asset is sold.
jobs.think: If ₹3 lakh of training cost stays capitalised in a 10-year asset (SLM, nil residual), by how much is the current year's profit overstated?
jobs.answer: Expense of ₹3,00,000 is avoided and only ₹30,000 depreciation is charged on it, so profit is overstated by ₹2,70,000.

jobs.title: Laptops wear out faster than planned
jobs.role: Finance executive at an IT services company
jobs.situation: Laptops costing ₹60 lakh were being depreciated on SLM over 5 years with nil residual value. After 2 years, the IT head says they will last only 1 more year.
steps: Treat the revised life as a change in estimate: ₹36 lakh over the remaining 1 year.
Do not restate the previous two years.
Disclose the nature and amount of the change in the notes.
jobs.takeaway: Changes in life, residual value or method are prospective: re-spread the carrying amount from now on.

mcqs.q: Depreciation is best described as:
options: Spreading an asset's cost less residual value over its useful life in a systematic way
Fall in the market value of an asset
A fund created to replace an asset
A cash expense of the year
mcqs.explain: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of an asset's depreciable amount (cost less residual value) over its useful life, matching the cost of using the asset with the revenue it helps earn. It is a process of allocation, not valuation. The tempting option, 'fall in the market value', confuses depreciation with valuation — a building's market value may rise while it is still depreciated. It is also a non-cash expense. In practice: depreciation is added back to profit when computing cash flow from operations.
mcqs.topic: What depreciation is

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT included in the cost of a machine?
options: Freight to bring it to the factory
mcqs.explain: The cost of a machine includes costs directly attributable to bringing it to the location and condition needed for its intended use — installation, freight and the net cost of trial runs. An inauguration ceremony is a promotional or opening cost that adds nothing to the machine's working condition, so it is expensed. The tempting option, net cost of trial runs, is included because testing is needed before use. In practice: auditors reject attempts to capitalise launch events and opening ceremonies.
mcqs.topic: Measuring depreciation: cost, useful life, residual value

mcqs.q: Cost ₹5,40,000; residual value ₹40,000; life 5 years. SLM depreciation per year:
mcqs.explain: Under the straight line method, annual depreciation = (Cost − Residual value) ÷ Useful life = (₹5,40,000 − ₹40,000) ÷ 5 = ₹1,00,000. The tempting ₹1,08,000 divides the full cost by 5, ignoring the residual value that the business expects to recover at the end. In practice: most Indian companies use SLM over the useful lives indicated in Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013, typically assuming a residual value of up to 5% of cost.
mcqs.topic: Straight line and written down value methods

mcqs.q: A machine costing ₹4,00,000 is depreciated at 10% WDV. Depreciation for the second year:
mcqs.explain: Under WDV, the rate is applied each year to the opening written down value. Year 1: 10% × ₹4,00,000 = ₹40,000, leaving WDV ₹3,60,000. Year 2: 10% × ₹3,60,000 = ₹36,000. The tempting ₹40,000 applies the rate to original cost every year, which is the straight line method. In practice: the Income-tax Act computes depreciation on the WDV of each block of assets, so tax and book depreciation often differ.
mcqs.topic: Straight line and written down value methods

mcqs.q: Cost ₹5,00,000, residual value ₹2,04,800, life 4 years. The WDV rate that writes it down to residual value is:
mcqs.explain: The WDV rate that reduces cost to residual value over n years is r = 1 − (Residual value ÷ Cost)^(1/n) = 1 − (2,04,800 ÷ 5,00,000)^(1/4) = 1 − (0.4096)^(1/4) = 1 − 0.8 = 20%. Check: 5,00,000 × 0.8⁴ = 2,04,800. The tempting 25% divides 100% by 4 years — that is an SLM-style rate and would write the asset down far below ₹2,04,800. In practice: companies use this formula to convert Schedule II useful lives into WDV rates.
mcqs.topic: Straight line and written down value methods

mcqs.q: Under the sum of years' digits method for a 4-year life, first-year depreciation is what fraction of the depreciable amount?
mcqs.explain: Under the sum of years' digits method, the denominator is the sum of the digits of the useful life: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. Each year's charge uses the remaining life at the start of that year as the numerator, so year 1 = 4/10, year 2 = 3/10, and so on. The tempting 1/4 is the straight line fraction. In practice: SYD front-loads depreciation, suiting assets such as vehicles and computers that lose usefulness quickly in early years.
mcqs.topic: Other methods: SYD, machine hour, production units, depletion

mcqs.q: Depreciable amount ₹24,00,000; estimated 60,000 hours; machine worked 7,500 hours this year. Depreciation:
mcqs.explain: Under the machine hour method, rate per hour = Depreciable amount ÷ Estimated total hours = ₹24,00,000 ÷ 60,000 = ₹40 per hour. Depreciation = 7,500 hours × ₹40 = ₹3,00,000. The tempting ₹4,00,000 uses ₹24,00,000 ÷ 6, as if the machine's life were measured in years, ignoring actual usage. In practice: machine hour rates suit heavy equipment whose wear depends on running time, such as construction machinery hired out by the hour.
mcqs.topic: Other methods: SYD, machine hour, production units, depletion

mcqs.q: A mine is acquired for ₹1,20,00,000 with 4,00,000 tonnes extractable. 25,000 tonnes are extracted this year. Depletion:
mcqs.explain: Depletion is used for wasting assets such as mines. Rate per tonne = ₹1,20,00,000 ÷ 4,00,000 tonnes = ₹30. Depletion = 25,000 tonnes × ₹30 = ₹7,50,000. The tempting ₹12,00,000 spreads cost evenly over an assumed 10-year life, ignoring that the mine's value is used up by extraction, not by the passage of time. In practice: coal, limestone and iron ore mining companies in India charge depletion on a units-of-production basis.
mcqs.topic: Other methods: SYD, machine hour, production units, depletion

mcqs.q: An asset with a carrying amount of ₹2,40,000 on 1 April is sold on 1 October for ₹2,00,000. Depreciation is 10% WDV. Loss on sale:
mcqs.explain: Depreciation is charged up to the date of sale: 10% × ₹2,40,000 × 6/12 = ₹12,000, so the carrying amount on 1 October = ₹2,28,000. Loss = ₹2,28,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹28,000. The tempting ₹40,000 compares the sale price with the opening carrying amount, forgetting six months' depreciation. In practice: fixed asset registers in ERP systems calculate depreciation to the date of disposal automatically before computing profit or loss on sale.
mcqs.topic: Disposal of an asset — profit or loss

mcqs.q: A change in the estimated useful life of an asset is treated as:
options: A change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively
A change in accounting policy, applied retrospectively
mcqs.explain: A change in useful life is a revision of an estimate based on new information, so it is a change in accounting estimate. It is applied prospectively: the remaining carrying amount is spread over the revised remaining life, and past figures are not restated. The tempting option, a change in accounting policy applied retrospectively, would wrongly reopen earlier years. In practice: companies disclose revised useful lives and their effect on current-year depreciation in the notes to accounts.
mcqs.topic: Changes in method, useful life and residual value

mcqs.q: Cost ₹6,00,000, SLM over 10 years with nil residual value, for 3 years; remaining life is then revised to 5 years. Depreciation for year 4:
mcqs.explain: Annual SLM charge = ₹6,00,000 ÷ 10 = ₹60,000. After 3 years the carrying amount is ₹6,00,000 − ₹1,80,000 = ₹4,20,000. Spread over the revised remaining life of 5 years: ₹4,20,000 ÷ 5 = ₹84,000. The tempting ₹1,20,000 divides the original cost by 5, ignoring depreciation already charged. In practice: when engineers report a shorter remaining life, the accountant revises the charge from the current year without restating past years.
mcqs.topic: Changes in method, useful life and residual value

mcqs.q: On the first revaluation of an asset, a decrease in its carrying amount is:
options: Charged to the profit and loss account
Ignored until the asset is sold
mcqs.explain: Under AS 10, when an asset is revalued for the first time and its carrying amount decreases, there is no earlier revaluation surplus for that asset to absorb the decrease, so it is charged to the profit and loss account as an expense. The tempting option, debiting revaluation surplus, applies only if a surplus from an earlier upward revaluation of the same asset exists. In practice: companies revaluing land or buildings recognise downward revaluations as losses, but upward ones in revaluation surplus.
mcqs.topic: Revaluation of PPE

mcqs.q: If an entity revalues one item of plant, it must:
options: Revalue the entire class of plant
Revalue all its assets of every class
Revalue it only once in its life
mcqs.explain: If one item of property, plant and equipment is revalued, the entire class to which it belongs must be revalued. This prevents selective revaluation — revaluing only items that have gained in value — and avoids mixing costs and values from different dates within a class. The tempting option, 'revalue only that item', is exactly what the rule forbids. In practice: a company revaluing one factory building must revalue all its buildings, typically using an independent registered valuer.
mcqs.topic: Revaluation of PPE

mcqs.q: Which of these is NOT an intangible asset?
mcqs.explain: To be an intangible asset, an item must be identifiable, non-monetary and have no physical form. Trade receivables are monetary assets — rights to receive fixed amounts of money — so they are not intangible assets even though they cannot be touched. The tempting option, airport landing slots, sounds unusual but is a classic intangible: an identifiable right with no physical form. In practice: airlines such as IndiGo hold slot rights, while receivables are shown separately as financial assets.
mcqs.topic: Intangible assets

mcqs.q: Unless there is evidence to the contrary, the useful life of an intangible asset is presumed not to exceed:
mcqs.explain: AS 26 presumes, unless evidence shows otherwise, that an intangible asset's useful life is at most 10 years, counted from when it becomes available for use. A longer life may be used only with clear evidence. The tempting 20 years was a presumption in some older international rules, but AS 26 uses 10 years. In practice: Indian companies following AS typically amortise software and licences over 3–10 years, disclosing reasons if they use more than 10 years.
mcqs.topic: Amortisation

mcqs.q: Streaming rights cost ₹18,00,000 for 10 years (SLM). At the start of year 4 the remaining life is revised to 6 years. Amortisation for year 4:
mcqs.explain: Annual amortisation was ₹18,00,000 ÷ 10 = ₹1,80,000. After 3 years the carrying amount is ₹18,00,000 − ₹5,40,000 = ₹12,60,000. With a revised remaining life of 6 years: ₹12,60,000 ÷ 6 = ₹2,10,000 for year 4. The tempting ₹3,00,000 divides the original cost by 6, ignoring amortisation already charged. In practice: OTT platforms revise amortisation of content rights when viewership falls faster than expected.
mcqs.topic: Amortisation

summary: Depreciation = systematic spreading of (cost − residual value) over useful life; an allocation, not a valuation; non-cash.
Causes: wear and tear, passage of time, obsolescence, fall in market value, depletion. Starts when available for use.
Cost of PPE: price less trade discount + non-refundable taxes + directly attributable costs + dismantling estimate. Not: inauguration, advertising, training, admin, idle-time costs, relocation.
Methods: SLM (constant), WDV (falling), SYD, machine hour, production units, depletion.
Disposal: depreciate to date of sale; profit/loss = proceeds − carrying amount.
Change in method / life / residual value = change in estimate — prospective.
Revaluation: whole class; increase → revaluation surplus; decrease → P&L (subject to reversals).
Intangibles: identifiable, control, probable benefits, reliable cost; amortise, presumed life ≤ 10 years, SLM if pattern unclear, residual nil normally.
remember: Part-year: count months available for use.
Provision method: asset stays at cost; accumulated depreciation is transferred to the disposal account on sale.
traps: Don't skip depreciation for the part-year before a sale.
Don't capitalise training or inauguration costs.
Don't restate past years for a change in estimate.
Don't credit a revaluation increase to profit (unless it reverses an earlier charge).

viva.q: What is depreciation? Is it a method of valuing an asset?
viva.model: Depreciation means spreading the depreciable amount of an asset, that is its cost less residual value, systematically over its useful life. It is a process of allocation of cost, not of valuation, so it does not show the market value of the asset. It is a non-cash expense.

viva.q: Distinguish between the straight line method and the written down value method.
viva.model: Under the straight line method depreciation is charged at the same amount every year on the original cost, and the asset can be written down to nil or its residual value. viva.model: An intangible asset is a non-monetary asset that can be identified separately and has no physical substance; it is held for use in production or supply of goods or services, for rental or for administration. cases.title: Nova Prints — a press bought, used and sold
cases.case: Nova Prints (year-end 31 March) bought a printing press on 1 July 2025 for ₹11,50,000 and paid ₹50,000 for installation. It charges depreciation at 20% p.a. on the written down value. On 1 April 2027 the press was sold for ₹9,00,000. No provision for depreciation account is kept.

mcqs.q: Depreciation for 2025-26 is:
mcqs.explain: Cost = price ₹11,50,000 + installation ₹50,000 = ₹12,00,000. The press was used from 1 July 2025 to 31 March 2026, so 9 months' depreciation: ₹12,00,000 × 20% × 9/12 = ₹1,80,000. The tempting ₹2,40,000 charges a full year although the press was bought in July; ₹1,72,500 leaves out installation from cost. In practice: companies charge depreciation from the date an asset is ready for use, on a pro-rata basis.
mcqs.topic: Straight line and written down value methods

mcqs.q: Depreciation for 2026-27 is:
mcqs.explain: Under WDV, the rate applies to the opening written down value. WDV on 1 April 2026 = ₹12,00,000 − ₹1,80,000 = ₹10,20,000. Depreciation for 2026-27 = 20% × ₹10,20,000 = ₹2,04,000. The tempting ₹2,40,000 applies 20% to the original cost, which is the straight line approach. In practice: the WDV charge falls each year, which is why tax rules for plant and machinery use WDV on blocks of assets.
mcqs.topic: Straight line and written down value methods

mcqs.q: The carrying amount on 1 April 2027 is:
mcqs.explain: Carrying amount = cost − accumulated depreciation = ₹12,00,000 − ₹1,80,000 (2025-26) − ₹2,04,000 (2026-27) = ₹8,16,000. The tempting ₹7,68,000 assumes a full year's depreciation in 2025-26 (₹12,00,000 × 0.8 × 0.8), ignoring that the press was bought in July. In practice: the carrying amount in the fixed asset register is the starting point for working out profit or loss when an asset is sold.
mcqs.topic: Disposal of an asset — profit or loss

mcqs.q: The result of the sale is:
mcqs.explain: Profit or loss on sale = proceeds − carrying amount = ₹9,00,000 − ₹8,16,000 = profit of ₹84,000, credited to profit and loss. No depreciation is charged for 2027-28 because the press was sold on the first day of that year. The tempting 'loss ₹84,000' reverses the comparison; proceeds exceed the carrying amount, so it is a profit. In practice: such profits appear under other income, while the proceeds appear under investing activities in the cash flow statement.
mcqs.topic: Disposal of an asset — profit or loss
